name: Fence material
seoDesc: Fence material: work out number of posts from the fence length and the post space. A free construction calculator with the formula, units and a worked…
summary: Supply the fence length, the post space, number of rails and the picket width and the Fence material calculator solves for number of posts. That makes it useful for a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Fence material calculator work?
sections.html:
The Fence material calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports number of posts in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the post shape); then you type in the fence length, the post space, number of rails and the picket width.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Fence material calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Number of posts=rounded up, ((fence length + post space) ÷ post space)
Number of sections=rounded up, (fence length ÷ post space)
Rails per section=number of rails ÷ rounded up, (fence length ÷ post space)
Number of pickets=rounded up, (fence length ÷ (picket spacing + picket width))
Fence height=(2 ÷ 3) × post length
Post length=(3 ÷ 2) × concrete volume ÷ (PI × (post diameter ^ 2) × rounded up, ((fence length + post space) ÷ post space))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Fence length = 30 m, Post space = 30 m, Rails per section = 2 and Picket width = 30 cm. The calculator returns Number of posts = 2, Number of sections = 1, Number of rails = 2 and Number of pickets = 1.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Number of posts = 2, Number of sections = 1, Number of rails = 2 and Number of pickets = 1 should be roughly the size you expected from Fence length = 30 m and Post space = 30 m.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Fence material calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the fence length, the post space and number of rails — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Fence material calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns number of posts, derived from the fence length, the post space and number of rails. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Fence material calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the fence length, the post space, number of rails and the picket width, which is 10 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter fence length in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Fence length opens in meters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Number of posts = 2. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Fence material calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
